To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the asymptotic behavior of the generalization error of kernel methods is independent of the kernel, and that the effective smoothness of data, as measured in the Teacher-Student paradigm, is related to the effective dimensionality of the data.

(1) for real data, the generalization error  of kernel regression and classification decays as a power law with exponent that is independent of the specific choice of kernel, and (2) this exponent is the same for regression and classification tasks.

i) the exponent $\beta$ that governs the learning curves is the same for regression and classification, and for different kernels; ii) $\beta$ can be predicted analytically in the Teacher-Student setting, and iii) the predictions are in good agreement with empirical data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental problem of how much data is needed to learn a given task.
the fundamental problem of how much training data are needed for supervised learning.
the fundamental problem of how many training data are required for learning a task.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the asymptotic learning curves of the Teacher-Student paradigm are in good agreement with the empirical ones, at least for the cases we have studied.
the learning curve of kernel methods on real data is not universal and it is not possible to predict it a priori.
kernel methods can learn from a number of data points that grows as $\sim n^{\beta}$, where $\beta$ depends on the data and the kernel, and can be predicted by our Teacher-Student paradigm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for kernel methods, the relevant smoothness of the data is defined by the distance between the nearest data points, and not by the intrinsic dimension of the data.
, when using a kernel method to learn a task, the relevant dimension of  the data is  the number of data points needed to span the space of functions  that are needed to perform the task.

, for kernel methods, the number of data points $n$ needed to learn the task is not determined by the dimension $d$ of the data, but by a quantity $\mathcal{D}$ that is a function of $n$ and $d$, and that is related to the effective smoothness of the data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the asymptotic learning curves of kernels are universal in the sense that they depend only on the data, and not on the specific kernel used.
the asymptotic behavior of the learning curve is determined by the smoothness of the data, and not by the specific kernel used.
the Teacher-Student paradigm is a useful tool to understand the learning curves of kernel algorithms.
